q: Where is the crossover from the empirically-observed flat shot budget (<=4 queries for |G|<=15) to the theoretical polylog-|G| shot growth predicted by Watrous, and what are the leading constants inside the continued-fraction success probability that govern this crossover?
basis: Our scaling table (report/evidence/results/results.json, demo3_scaling) shows shots-to-success of 1-4 across N in [6,15], plotting flat rather than log-growing. Without pushing to N in the thousands we cannot see the polylog regime; Aer statevector can go to ~24 qubits (N ~ 4096) which would produce a real crossover plot.
next_steps: Extend the scaling script to N in {32, 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024, 4096}, generalize the oracle unitary to sparse-matrix form to save memory beyond t=12, and fit shots(N) to a poly(log N) model. Confirm or refute the flat-empirical-cost observation.

q: How does the trace distance of the prepared uniform state |G> degrade under a depolarizing black-box oracle at rate p per query, as a joint function of |G| and the derived-series length of G?
basis: Watrous's Theorem 1 assumes an exact oracle. Our replication achieves trace distance <= 2e-8 with a perfect statevector oracle, but real hardware would deliver noisy oracles. The paper does not analyze how noise propagates through the recursion, and near-term hardware makes this newly answerable.
next_steps: Wrap the oracle unitary with a Kraus depolarizing channel of rate p in Qiskit Aer's density-matrix mode, sweep p in [1e-4, 1e-2] and re-measure trace distance for cyclic Z_N (derived length 1) vs D_4 (length 2) vs iterated dihedral (length 3+). Extract a scaling law and compare to a resource estimate for IBM/Quantinuum hardware.

q: When the black-box group is presented as permutations of {0,...,m-1} with m strictly greater than |G|, what is the minimum ancilla + query cost to project onto the group subspace when preparing |G>, and does it depend on whether the presentation is random-Cayley vs. polycyclic?
basis: Our D_4 encoding is loss-less (|G|=8=2^3), which sidesteps the black-box padding issue Watrous actually operates in. Real solvable-group inputs (e.g., a subgroup of a permutation representation) have m > |G| and require projection. The paper handles this abstractly but does not give explicit ancilla counts.
next_steps: Reimplement |G> preparation for a padded encoding (e.g., D_4 embedded in S_5 permutations, m=120), measure the ancilla count and success probability of the projection step, and compare polycyclic (structured) vs. random-Cayley presentations.

q: Does error accumulation across the derived-series recursion force the sampling-register width to grow linearly in derived length, i.e., t = O(ell * log|G|), rather than the O(log|G|) that suffices at each individual level?
basis: We ran the atomic HSP subroutine with t = 2 log2 N and it succeeded on 8/8 cyclic cases (derived length 1). Watrous's Section 3 gives asymptotic guarantees but never a tight bound on the per-level t needed to keep the composed error <= epsilon after ell levels. Empirically testing iterated wreath products (controllable derived length) would settle this.
next_steps: Build a controlled family of solvable groups with derived length ell = 1, 2, 3, 4 (e.g., iterated Z_2-wreath), implement the two-level composed HSP (invocation of parent HSP with a subroutine call to the child HSP), and measure the minimum t at level 1 required to keep composed success rate >= 0.9.

q: For the smallest non-abelian solvable groups (D_n for n<=8, Q_8, S_3, A_4), what is the minimum T-count / CNOT-count reversible circuit compilation of the group-operation oracle, and does it beat the Theta(|G|^2) lookup-table circuit we used?
basis: Our HSP replication implements the oracle as a full permutation UnitaryGate of size (2^t * 2^ceil(log2 d))^2, i.e., Theta(|G|^2) classical memory. This is fine for demonstration but incompatible with Watrous's polynomial claim on any actual quantum hardware, where oracle depth must be poly(log |G|). The paper defers to 'assume the oracle is efficient' but doesn't produce one.
next_steps: For each small solvable group, hand-compile the Cayley-table permutation into a Clifford+T circuit (candidates: Reed-Muller reversible synthesis, or ancilla-augmented Toffoli networks). Compare gate-count against 2^(2t) and against known permutation-synthesis bounds. This would produce the first end-to-end resource estimate for Watrous's algorithm on the smallest non-trivial case.
